title: Why Do Wolves Howl? It Is Not About the Moon
summary:
Picture a wolf lifting its head and letting out a long, spooky howl. But wolves are not howling at the moon. That is a myth, says zoologist Arik Kershenbaum of the University of Cambridge. So why do they do it? Experts told Live Science that howling is really about keeping in touch.

Wolves can bark and growl, but the howl is their long-distance call. A lone wolf may howl to find its pack again, a new pack, or a mate.

When a whole pack howls together, it tells rival packs: this land is taken. Packs howl more in the middle of their land, when pups are near, and when they have food, says Tamás Faragó of Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest. Most group howling is social.

One wolf often answers another's howl. But a lone wolf in a neighbour's land stays quiet, or it would give itself away. A howl can be heard up to 10 miles (16 kilometres) away, says the Wolf Conservation Center in South Salem, New York. Wolf pups try to howl when they are 2 to 4 weeks old.
why_it_matters: Next time you hear a wolf howl in a film or at a zoo, you will know it is really a wolf talking to its family.

background_read: Wolves live in family groups called packs, and each pack has its own land.
Howling is a long, loud call that can travel very far, so wolves use it to talk to each other across the wild.
A howl can tell other wolves where a pack is, warn rivals away, or help a lost wolf find its family again.
Article_Structure: WHO: Wolves, wolf pups, and experts like zoologist Arik Kershenbaum and Tamás Faragó.
WHAT: Wolves howl to keep in touch with each other, not at the moon.
WHERE: In the wild, across a pack's land.
WHY: Howling helps wolves find each other, warn rival packs away, and stay close as a family.
